prompt: A hypothetical open-pit gold project is assessed at a gold price of US$2,500/oz. Inputs: head grade 0.90 g/t Au; metallurgical recovery 90%; selling cost (refining, transport, royalty) US$60/oz sold; processing plus site G&A US$32.00 per tonne of ore; mining cost US$4.20 per tonne of material moved (the same unit cost for ore and waste). The optimised pit has a life-of-mine average strip ratio of 4.9 t waste per t ore. The planning team proposes a final pushback that adds 6.0 Mt of ore at 0.90 g/t and 43.2 Mt of waste (7.2 t waste per t ore), arguing it is justified because the pit average of 4.9:1 remains below the break-even strip ratio. Use 31.1035 g per troy ounce and ignore capital, sustaining capital and discounting. (a) Calculate the break-even strip ratio at these inputs. (b) Assess the pushback argument and say whether you would approve the pushback.
reference_answer: (a) Net revenue per tonne of ore = 0.90 g/t x 0.90 / 31.1035 x (2,500 - 60) = US$63.54/t. Less processing/G&A 32.00 and ore mining 4.20 leaves a margin available to pay for stripping of US$27.34 per tonne of ore. Each tonne of waste costs 4.20, so the break-even strip ratio is 27.34 / 4.20 = 6.51 t waste per t ore. (b) The argument confuses the average with the margin. The pushback must be judged on its own incremental strip ratio. At 7.2:1 the waste cost is 7.2 x 4.20 = US$30.24 per tonne of ore against a margin of US$27.34, so each ore tonne loses about US$2.90 and the 6.0 Mt pushback loses about US$17.4 M before capital and discounting. The earlier, lower-strip layers of the pit are already paid for; the average staying below break-even is irrelevant to the decision to mine the last increment. Do not approve at these inputs. A higher gold price, higher recovery, or a lower unit mining cost would be needed (the break-even is sensitive: it moves roughly with price x recovery, and mining cost rises with depth, which makes 4.20 optimistic for a final pushback). Capital for the pushback, pre-strip timing and discounting would make it worse.

rubric.criterion: Concludes the pushback should not be approved because its incremental strip ratio (7.2:1) exceeds the break-even strip ratio (about 6.5:1).
Explains that the decision for a pushback is marginal (incremental strip versus break-even), so the pit-average strip ratio staying below break-even is not a valid argument.
Calculates a break-even strip ratio of about 6.5:1 using net revenue per tonne less processing and ore-mining cost, divided by the unit waste mining cost.
Notes that the result ignores capital, discounting and cost rising with depth, and that it is sensitive to price, recovery and mining cost.

prompt: A hypothetical scoping study for an orogenic gold project in West Africa reports 28.0 Mt of Inferred and Indicated material: 6.0 Mt of oxide cap at 1.60 g/t Au and 22.0 Mt of fresh sulphide at 2.10 g/t Au. The study applies a single flowsheet to all ore: whole-ore grinding and carbon-in-leach (CIL) at 90% gold recovery and US$19/t processing cost. Metallurgical testwork reported in an appendix: oxide composites, direct CIL 92%. Sulphide composites (four): direct whole-ore CIL 38% (range 31-44%). Mineralogy by automated mineralogy with laser-ablation ICP-MS mapping of the sulphides: gold in sulphide ore is mainly submicroscopic within arsenopyrite and pyrite, with 2.4% total sulphur and 1.1% arsenic. A flotation test on sulphide ore gave 7% mass pull to a concentrate carrying 90% of the gold; pressure oxidation (POX) of that concentrate followed by CIL extracted 95% of the contained gold. Indicative costs: flotation plus grinding US$21/t of ore; POX/neutralisation/CIL on concentrate US$190/t of concentrate. Use 31.1035 g per troy ounce. (a) Calculate recovered gold from the sulphide ore under the study's assumption, under direct CIL as tested, and under the flotation-plus-POX route. (b) Calculate the processing cost per tonne of sulphide ore on the flotation-plus-POX route and the extra cost over the study's allowance for the 22.0 Mt. (c) Assess the study's recovery and processing assumptions.
reference_answer: (a) Sulphide contained gold = 22.0 Mt x 2.10 g/t = 46.2 t = 1485.4 koz. Study assumption (90%): 1336.8 koz. Direct CIL as tested (38%): 564.4 koz. Flotation (90%) x POX/CIL (95%) = 85.5%: 1270.0 koz. (b) Route cost per tonne ore = 21 + 0.07 x 190 = US$34.3/t versus the study's US$19/t, an extra US$15.3/t or about US$337 M over 22.0 Mt (before the capital cost of a flotation plant and POX autoclave and arsenic management). (c) The study treats a refractory sulphide ore like the free-milling oxide cap. The mineralogy (submicroscopic gold in arsenopyrite and pyrite) predicts the poor direct-CIL result; the 90% assumption is supported only for the oxide cap and overstates sulphide recovered gold by about 137% relative to testwork at 38%. A refractory route can recover most of the gold (about 85% overall) but at roughly 1.8 times the unit processing cost, plus POX capital, and it requires arsenic fixation and tailings/effluent permits. The project should be re-scoped as a two-stage case: oxide cap on CIL early, then sulphide through a refractory circuit, with the cut-off grade recalculated for each ore type (the sulphide cut-off rises with the higher cost). The sulphide economics may still work at 2.1 g/t, but the study as written is not a sound basis. Also note the study mixes Inferred and Indicated material without giving the split, so any scoping economics need the Inferred proportion and sequencing disclosed.

rubric.criterion: Identifies that the sulphide ore is refractory (submicroscopic gold in arsenopyrite and pyrite) and that the single 90% free-milling recovery applied to all ore is unsupported by the testwork (about 38% direct CIL).

States that the supported route for the sulphide ore requires concentration and oxidation (flotation plus POX or equivalent), giving about 85% overall recovery at a materially higher unit cost and capital.
Quantifies the extra processing cost (about US$34/t vs US$19/t) or the recovered-gold shortfall under direct CIL.
Recommends separate oxide and sulphide process routes and cut-off grades, and notes arsenic management and permitting.

prompt: A hypothetical alluvial gold project on a floodplain terrace in South America has an Indicated resource of 2.4 million bank cubic metres (bcm) of gravel at 0.35 g/m3 Au. The pre-feasibility design is a trommel and jig wash plant processing 200 bcm/h for 6,000 h/yr (1.2 Mbcm/yr) at 85% gold recovery, with annual operating cost of US$13.0 M, treated as largely independent of throughput, and a gold price of US$2,400/oz. A 40-day pilot plant run on the same plant type, on bulk samples from three trenches, logged a throughput of 110 bcm/h and 72% recovery. The trench logs show the gravel matrix contains about 25% by mass of clay and silt, with clay balls reported in the scrubber discharge. Use 31.1035 g per troy ounce and assume the pilot throughput and recovery hold for the full-scale plant. (a) Calculate annual recovered ounces for the design case and the pilot case. (b) Calculate the pilot-case annual revenue and margin after the operating cost, and the mine life at the pilot throughput. (c) Assess what the pilot result means for the project.
reference_answer: (a) Design: 200 x 6,000 = 1.2 Mbcm x 0.35 g/m3 = 420 kg x 0.85 = 357 kg = 11478 oz/yr. Pilot: 110 x 6,000 = 0.66 Mbcm x 0.35 = 231 kg x 0.72 = 166.3 kg = 5347 oz/yr (about 47% of design). (b) Pilot revenue = 5347 oz x US$2,400 = US$12.8 M, less operating cost 13.0 gives US$-0.2 M, i.e. no margin. Mine life at 0.66 Mbcm/yr = 2.4 / 0.66 = 3.6 years instead of 2.0, with fixed costs spread over fewer ounces. (c) The pilot shows two clay effects that the design grade-times-throughput arithmetic misses: clay and silt matrix slows the wash plant (scrubbing, screening blinding, clay balls that carry gold into oversize), cutting throughput to 55% of design, and gold locked in clay balls and slimes lowers recovery. The two multiply, so ounces per year fall by more than half. The project is uneconomic at the tested plant configuration. Options: add a log washer or attritioning scrubber and pre-screening to break clay and recover gold from clay balls, retest, and re-cost the capital; test a bigger plant to restore annual ounces; and require a bulk-sample-based throughput and recovery by sub-area (clay content probably varies across the terrace). Grade per m3 alone, however well sampled, is not the value driver here; matrix and clay content determine plant capacity and recovery. A resource of 2.4 Mbcm at 0.35 g/m3 should not be presented as ounces recoverable at 85% without that disclosure.

rubric.criterion: Identifies the clay-rich matrix (25% clay and silt, clay balls) as the cause of reduced plant throughput and recovery relative to the design assumptions.
Calculates that pilot-case recovered gold is about 5,300 oz/yr versus about 11,500 oz/yr in the design case (roughly 47%).
Concludes the pilot-case annual margin is about zero or negative at the stated operating cost and gold price, so the project is not viable as designed.
Recommends a remedy or further work such as scrubbing/log-washing or attritioning, clay-ball treatment, retesting, and sub-area bulk sampling for clay content.

prompt: A hypothetical preliminary economic assessment (PEA) for a heap-leach gold project in a semi-arid region schedules 30.0 Mt of Inferred and Indicated material, mined from a single pit: oxide 8.0 Mt at 1.10 g/t Au, transition 5.0 Mt at 1.00 g/t, fresh sulphide 17.0 Mt at 0.95 g/t. Oxide is mined in years 1-3 and the deeper material in years 4-12. The PEA applies a single heap-leach gold recovery of 78% to all material, citing column leach tests at a 12.5 mm crush. The column-test appendix reports: oxide composites 80%; transition composites 55% and 49%; fresh sulphide composites 30% and 26%. The PEA also applies a single cut-off grade of 0.30 g/t, a heap-leach operating cost (including G&A) of US$11/t of ore and a gold price of US$2,400/oz, with selling costs of US$50/oz. Use 31.1035 g per troy ounce. (a) Calculate contained gold, recovered gold under the PEA's 78% assumption, and recovered gold using the column-test averages by material type. (b) Calculate the cut-off grade for each material type using the column-test recoveries. (c) Assess the PEA.
reference_answer: (a) Contained gold: oxide 8.0 Mt x 1.10 = 8.8 t = 282.9 koz; transition 5.0 x 1.00 = 160.8 koz; sulphide 17.0 x 0.95 = 16.15 t = 519.2 koz; total 962.9 koz. PEA at 78%: 751.1 koz. Column-test recovered gold: oxide x 0.80 = 226.3, transition x 0.52 = 83.6, sulphide x 0.28 = 145.4, total 455.3 koz. The PEA overstates recovered gold by 65% (751.1 vs 455.3 koz). (b) Cut-off grade = cost / (recovery x net price per g): oxide 11 / (0.80 x 2,350/31.1035) = 0.18 g/t; transition (52%) 0.28 g/t; sulphide (28%) 0.52 g/t. The sulphide average of 0.95 g/t is only 1.8x its cut-off before mining cost and stripping and a single 0.30 g/t cut-off is too low for the deeper material. (c) The 78% is an oxide-only number extended to transition and fresh rock, where unoxidised sulphides encapsulate gold and heap-leach recovery falls sharply. The heap-leach plan is sound for the oxide cap (years 1-3) only. Beyond that, recoveries are about two thirds (transition) or about a third (sulphide) of the study value, so the plan should treat the deeper material either as waste, as a separate stockpile awaiting a mill/oxidation route with its own capital, or not at all. Year 4-12 recovered gold is overstated by more than double (about 16.5 t at 78% against 7.1 t on column-test recoveries), the PEA has no mill capital for a different flowsheet, and any Inferred portion must be flagged. Recovery should be carried by material type in the block model (oxidation state coded from logging and sulphur/CN-soluble assays) and cut-off grades recalculated by type.

rubric.criterion: Identifies that the 78% heap-leach recovery was derived from oxide samples and has been wrongly applied to transition and fresh sulphide material, where column tests show roughly 52% and 28%.
Quantifies the overstatement: recovered gold is about 455 koz on column-test recoveries against about 751 koz in the PEA (roughly 65% overstated).

Concludes the heap-leach plan is only supported for the oxide cap in years 1-3 and the years 4-12 material needs a different flowsheet (mill, oxidation) or should be excluded, with capital and cost implications.

Notes that cut-off grade must be calculated by material type using recovery for each (e.g. about 0.18 g/t oxide, 0.28 g/t transition, 0.52 g/t sulphide on processing cost alone), not one 0.30 g/t cut-off.
Flags that the PEA relies on Inferred material and that a recovery by material type should be carried in the block model.
